query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an active-learning–trained ML interatomic potential into a thermodynamic integration framework with selective ab initio corrections can yield fusion free energies (and derived high-temperature thermodynamic properties) that are within 5% of full ab initio MD results while reducing computational cost by at least an order of magnitude.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid phases near their melting points, where all vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects are fully captured.
generation.intervention: Train ML interatomic potentials on strategically selected ab initio MD snapshots in regions critical to the phase transition, then employ these ML models within a thermodynamic integration scheme that periodically corrects the ML predictions with ab initio evaluations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions around fusion (within ±10–20% of the experimental melting point) and compositions ranging from elemental and binary alloys up to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The accurate reproduction of free-energy surfaces that embody vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling through selectively corrected ML evaluations.
generation.mechanism: Active learning refines the ML potential in the most critical regions of the free-energy landscape where phase transition physics is complex, enabling rapid interpolation of ab initio energies and forces while periodic ab initio corrections maintain the fidelity of entropy contributions. This hybrid method reduces computational workload while preserving necessary physical details.
generation.predicted_outcome: A workflow that computes fusion free energies with deviations of less than 5% from full ab initio MD values, achieving at least an order-of-magnitude speed-up relative to full ab initio MD and improved scalability over TOR-TILD for high-entropy systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio MD free-energy evaluations and TOR-TILD calculations, which although accurate, are either computationally expensive or scale poorly for complex multicomponent systems.
generation.boundary: Applicability from simple elemental and binary systems up to complex high-entropy alloys; temperature regimes near the melting point (±10–20% around the experimental melting temperature) are targeted. Limitations may occur in systems with extreme configurational disorder not well sampled by initial ab initio snapshots.
generation.uncertainty: The degree to which the ML potential can fully capture the subtleties of electron–vibration coupling and extreme anharmonic effects—especially in highly disordered multicomponent alloys—remains to be fully established and may require more refined ab initio corrections.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the ML-accelerated thermodynamic integration approach to a suite of benchmark systems (elemental, binary, and high-entropy alloys) near their melting transition. Compute phase free energies, melting temperatures, and latent heats, and compare these with values obtained via full ab initio MD simulations.
measurements: Phase free energy differences for solid and liquid phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the phase free energies or derived melting properties (e.g., melting temperature, latent heat) deviate by more than 5% from the full ab initio MD results across multiple benchmark systems, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

frame.system: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy systems undergoing fusion (melting) where both solid and liquid phases must be modeled with full ab initio fidelity (including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling).
frame.goal: To substantially reduce the computational cost of accurately obtaining fusion (melting) and high-temperature thermodynamic properties by obtaining faithful free energies (including all relevant entropy contributions) for both solid and fluid states.
frame.limitation: Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluations (via molecular dynamics) are computationally expensive and while methods like TOR-TILD improve throughput for simpler systems, they scale poorly when extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.

frame.regime: High-temperature conditions near the fusion (melting) transition, spanning the relevant composition and temperature ranges (with clear boundaries defined from prior elemental and binary studies up to complex high-entropy alloys).

frame.understanding: This hypothesis aims to elucidate how a hybrid computational framework can bypass the need for full-scale ab initio molecular dynamics while keeping all essential thermodynamic contributions intact.
frame.proposed_hypothesis: Introduce an integrated methodology that combines machine-learning (ML) interatomic potentials with an active-learning accelerated thermodynamic integration scheme. The strategy is to train ML potentials on strategically chosen ab initio molecular dynamics snapshots for both the solid and liquid phases, and then use these ML models to rapidly interpolate the free-energy surfaces with enforced physical constraints (e.g., preserving anharmonic behavior and electron–vibration coupling fingerprints through selective ab initio corrections). This approach should work because the ML potential, once accurately trained in the relevant configuration space, can reproduce the expensive ab initio energy and force evaluations at a fraction of the cost, while the active learning loop guarantees that the model is refined in regions critical to phase transition (where entropy contributions are major). The expected speed is an improvement by at least an order of magnitude over explicit ab initio MD, with fidelity matching or within a few percent of TOR-TILD for simpler systems and overtaking it in multicomponent high-entropy regimes. The composition boundaries would span from elemental and binary alloys to high-entropy alloys, with the temperature range defined around the melting (fusion) region (e.g., within ±10–20% of the experimental melting point). Supporting evidence from prior studies on elemental and binary systems shows that ML potentials can capture detailed free-energy landscapes, and preliminary work using hybrid approaches has demonstrated accurate synthesis of vibrational and anharmonic contributions. A decisive benchmark for falsification would be a systematic deviation of phase free energies and derived observables (e.g., melting temperature and latent heat) by more than 5% compared to full ab initio MD results across several compositions, indicating that the ML-accelerated integration fails to capture the necessary entropy and coupling effects.

decision.trend: Initial studies in this field used simplified empirical potentials or first‐principles approaches that concentrated on estimating phase‐transition temperatures without fully capturing the detailed free‐energy landscape—including the contributions from vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling. Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics approaches later emerged and provided a full description of these thermodynamic quantities, but their high computational demand limited their routine application. The TOR-TILD method then increased the throughput for elemental and binary systems while still retaining much of the ab initio fidelity; however, its performance degrades considerably for multicomponent high-entropy alloys. Thus, there has been a gradual progression from low‐fidelity, computationally inexpensive methods toward high‐fidelity but prohibitively expensive approaches, leaving the application to complex, multicomponent systems unresolved.
decision.unsolved: A scalable, cost-effective method to obtain fully faithful free energies (with vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions) for both solid and liquid phases near fusion in multicomponent high-entropy systems, without resorting to prohibitively expensive full ab initio MD.
decision.lever: Integrate active-learning–trained ML interatomic potentials into a thermodynamic integration framework with selective ab initio corrections
decision.why: By training ML potentials on strategically chosen ab initio MD snapshots—especially in the critical regions around phase transitions—and actively refining the model where the physics is most challenging, this approach can rapidly and accurately interpolate the free-energy surfaces. It promises at least an order-of-magnitude speed-up over full ab initio MD, while matching or even exceeding the fidelity of TOR-TILD in elemental and binary systems and scaling well to the complexity of high-entropy alloys.
